findings.issue_text: [BUG] The code depends on queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception, which were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13, but Sentry's supported Python runtimes (3.11/3.12) do not have either. On Python < 3.13, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 316) raises AttributeError ('Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown') inside its own try/except, so the blocked worker threads never wake from work_queue.get() and join(timeout=5.0) always times out; additionally the `except queue.ShutDown` reference would itself be an AttributeError if ever evaluated, since queue.ShutDown does not exist below 3.13. Every consumer shutdown in this mode degrades to abandoning 20+ live daemon threads.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() has no caller anywhere in the diff (production code or tests), making it ships-inert dead code. Passes the deletion test: removing it deletes an unused polling loop and its timeout parameter; nothing else needs updating. It will silently rot if queue semantics change.

[BUG] The worker's finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() unconditionally even when result_processor raised, so failed messages are treated as successfully processed and their offsets get committed. A failing result_processor causes the message to be silently dropped with at-most-once semantics, directly violating SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'; uptime check results are lost with no retry or DLQ. test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling in tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py asserts that NO commit happens after a failure, which is a property the code does not implement — the test can only pass by timing luck (the 1s commit loop racing test teardown), so it either encodes wrong behavior or is flaky.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but FixedQueuePool creates unbounded queue.Queue() instances, so no backpressure exists anywhere in the design. During a consumer stall or a slow result_processor (e.g. a DB outage in handle_result), arroyo keeps feeding submit() and every queue grows without bound, causing unbounded memory growth and eventual OOM of the consumer process; no acceptance criterion in the diff addresses max queue depth or what happens when a worker falls behind.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is defined but never called by any production code or test in this diff — ships-inert code. Dead code that the next maintainer must reason about (its 5s default timeout and busy-poll semantics suggest a shutdown-drain intent that was never wired into close()/shutdown()); either delete it or wire it into shutdown so pending items actually drain before worker threads are told to stop.

[ADVISORY] OffsetTracker.all_offsets grows without bound for any partition that has a permanently blocked offset, and get_committable_offsets re-scans the full range from last_committed+1 to max_offset every second via range() iteration. A single lost/never-submitted offset (e.g. a decoder path that skips add/complete asymmetry or a partition hole) pins the commit head forever while all_offsets accumulates every subsequent offset, degrading memory and making the 1-second commit loop scan an ever-growing range; no test in the diff covers long-lived blocked-gap behavior.

[ADVISORY] The FixedQueuePool (and its N worker threads) is constructed in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, before create_with_partitions is called, and a second commit thread is started per SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy instantiation. Every consumer process that merely constructs the factory in thread-queue-parallel mode spawns up to 20 daemon threads plus a commit thread even if the strategy is never created, and if create_with_partitions is invoked more than once on the same factory (as the Kafka integration test does by monkey-patching it) multiple commit threads share one pool and race on commit_function; nothing in the diff verifies single-consumer-per-factory is an invariant.

[ADVISORY] get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(group_key), whose result for str is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the group-to-queue mapping is not stable across processes or restarts. Ordering guarantees only hold within a single process lifetime; any future feature that assumes stable group-to-shard assignment across restarts or across multiple consumer processes (e.g. debugging which queue a subscription lands on, or cross-process dedup keyed by queue index) silently breaks; a stable hash (md5/zlib.crc32 on the key) costs one line and removes the trap.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit asserts committed[0].offset == 5 unconditionally, but earlier in the same test the equivalent assertion is guarded by 'if commits_made:', indicating the author knew commits may not have landed within the window. The unconditional Kafka committed-offset assertion makes this requires_kafka integration test timing-flaky (ONCE_PER_SECOND commit policy racing a 5-second _run_once loop), producing intermittent CI failures on a slow broker that will be dismissed as flakes rather than signal.

[BUG] The OrderedQueueWorker marks a failed work item's offset complete, so the docstring guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is not enforced and failed messages are committed as processed. When result_processor raises for an item (line ~148-152 catches Exception and the finally block at line 153-158 calls complete_offset), the offset becomes committable; the commit loop then advances past a message that was never processed, and that uptime result is permanently lost on restart/rebalance.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but the queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize), so the invariant is not enforced. If processing is slower than consumption, the pool queues grow without limit until memory exhaustion; arroyo's submit() never blocks, so the consumer keeps pulling from Kafka at full rate with zero backpressure.

[ADVISORY] get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(), which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the claimed invariant 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' only holds within one process lifetime, not across restarts/rebalances. After a consumer restart the group-to-queue mapping changes; any operator reasoning about per-queue load or shard stability (the documented 'consistent hashing') gets different assignment every deploy. Using a stable hash (e.g. md5 of the key) would make the documented property actually hold.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool spawns its worker threads in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, before create_with_partitions is ever called, so a factory constructed but never used (or constructed per-process in a multiprocessing parent) leaks 20 daemon threads. Any code path that instantiates UptimeResultsStrategyFactory in thread-queue-parallel mode but never builds a strategy (e.g. config validation, CLI dry runs, tests that don't call shutdown) starts 20 live threads; unlike the ThreadPoolExecutor/multiprocessing paths, the pool exists at construction rather than at strategy creation.

[ADVISORY] The new mode key for 'parallelism' is max_workers but the implementation maps it to queue count (num_queues=max_workers or 20), conflating two different knobs the surrounding modes treat distinctly. Operators tuning --max-workers based on the updated help text ('maximum amount of parallelism') get queue count, while actual parallelism is one-thread-per-queue; if max_workers is later applied per-queue (matching the other parallel modes' semantics), parallelism silently multiplies by 20.

[ADVISORY] ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest is large infrastructure-level test work (AdminClient topic creation, raw Producer, StreamProcessor._run_once loops, a second verification consumer) that tests arroyo/Kafka commit plumbing rather than this diff's logic, and its central assertion is conditional. The 'if commits_made:' guard (around the last_commit assertions) means the test passes with zero tracked commits as long as the final Kafka committed-offset check passes, so half the verification it was written for can silently never run; the test also reaches into private StreamProcessor._run_once/_shutdown, making it fragile against arroyo upgrades.

[ADVISORY] terminate() does not stop/join the commit thread (only close() does), and join() aliases close(), giving three shutdown entry points with divergent behavior. On terminate() (arroyo's hard-shutdown path) the commit thread can fire one more commit_function call concurrently with queue_pool.shutdown() racing worker completion; a caller relying on terminate() for fast exit still waits on nothing, but a caller relying on terminate() to stop committing gets a post-shutdown commit attempt.

[ADVISORY] OffsetTracker._get_partition_lock has a check-then-act race: two threads can both see no lock and both call setdefault (harmless with setdefault) but the unlocked get() path means partition_locks can be read while another thread mutates the dict, which is a latent RuntimeError ('dictionary changed size during iteration') under GIL-free builds. The tracker is documented as thread-safe, but the lock-lazy-init pattern is not atomic on free-threaded Python; on current CPython it works only by luck of the GIL. A dict populated up-front in __init__ (or per-partition lock via defaultdict) removes the race entirely.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so failed messages are marked as processed. A message whose processing raises (e.g. a DB error in handle_result) has its offset marked complete and becomes committable; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop then commits it, so the message is permanently lost on restart. This directly contradicts the class's stated guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, which asserts no commit after a processing failure — the code and the test's asserted invariant disagree (the test only passes on a timing race with the 1s commit loop).

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() swallows decoder exceptions and immediately marks the offset complete, silently dropping undecodable messages. A malformed payload (bad schema version, decode error in get_topic_codec deserialization) raises inside self.decoder, is caught by the bare except, and its offset is added+completed, so the commit loop advances past it: poison messages are silently skipped with only a log line, no DLQ, no metric — the at-least-once guarantee the strategy claims is broken for the decode path.

[ADVISORY] The strategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but the queues are unbounded queue.Queue with no maxsize, so no backpressure exists. If result processing stalls (slow DB, hung HTTP), the arroyo consumer thread keeps submit()-ing and all 20 queues grow without bound, materializing every WorkItem (including the full Message) in memory until OOM; the operator gets no signal until the process dies, defeating the stated design property.

[ADVISORY] terminate() sets shutdown_event but never joins the commit thread, so _commit_loop can invoke commit_function after terminate() returns. During arroyo's hard-shutdown path, a commit thread already inside shutdown_event.wait(1.0) can wake, call the arroyo Commit callback on a consumer that is being torn down, and either raise (caught and logged as 'Error in commit loop', masking real shutdown errors) or commit offsets racing with the processor teardown.

[ADVISORY] num_queues=max_workers or 20 silently changes effective parallelism to 20 for existing operators who left --max-workers unset. Previously 'parallel' mode with no --max-workers defaulted to a small/default thread count; any deployment enabling thread-queue-parallel without explicitly setting max_workers now spawns 20 worker threads per consumer process (20 DB connections/HTTP clients via result_processor), multiplying per-process resource use by 20 with no operator-visible knob tied to the old default.

[ADVISORY] Queue assignment uses built-in hash(group_key), which is salted per Python process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so group→queue mapping differs across processes and restarts. Per-queue-index metrics (worker_N spans, queue_depth by index) are not comparable across replicas or over time, and any future operator debugging that assumes stable queue↔group binding will be misled; within a single process ordering is preserved, so this is observability drift, not a correctness bug — but a stable hash (e.g. md5/int from hashlib) costs one line.

[ADVISORY] The worker emits a metrics.gauge for queue_depth on every processed item inside the finally block. On a hot uptime-results topic this is one gauge submission per message across 20 threads, adding hot-path overhead that scales with throughput rather than with poll cadence; poll() already reports total_queued periodically, so the per-item gauge duplicates it at much higher cost.

[ADVISORY] The try/except queue.ShutDown around result_processor is dead code: ShutDown can only be raised by work_queue.get(), which is already handled above. Next editor reading the second except assumes processing can raise ShutDown and relies on it; removing/consolidating the two handlers is a deletion-test win (one fewer branch to reason about).

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() is unused by any caller in the diff. Dead parallel shutdown-drain mechanism: if graceful drain semantics are ever needed they will be built a second time rather than wired here, and until then it implies a drain guarantee at shutdown that shutdown() does not actually provide.

[ADVISORY] all_offsets accumulates unboundedly per partition if any submitted offset is never completed (e.g. queue.put raising after add_offset, or a worker thread dying before finally). get_committable_offsets() starts from max(last_committed+1, min_offset) and stops at the first gap, so a permanently stuck offset freezes commits for that partition at the gap forever (head-of-line commit stall) while the all_offsets set for that partition grows without bound — a liveness cliff with no timeout or skip mechanism.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run swallows any exception from result_processor and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in the finally block, so failed messages are marked as processed. A message whose processing raises is permanently skipped: the offset becomes committable, the commit loop commits past it, and the record is never retried — silent data loss that directly contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Under the pre-existing serial/parallel modes a processing exception propagates into arroyo and the offset is not committed, so this new mode silently changes the delivery-semantics objective without any recorded human acceptance of at-most-once processing.

[BUG] The new test suite never exercises the failure path at the queue_consumer level, and the artifact's own integration test (tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling) asserts the opposite of what the implementation does, so the tests and code disagree on the error objective. With mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception(...), None], the worker swallows the exception at offset 100 and completes it in finally, so both offsets become committable and commit_function fires with 102 (+1 semantics); the test asserts 'len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets' and therefore fails (or, if timing masks it, encodes an unaccepted at-most-once objective). One side of this artifact is definitively wrong and no review iteration resolved which.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but queues are constructed unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) and submit() never blocks, so there is no backpressure mechanism anywhere in the diff. When result processing is slower than consumption (e.g., a slow downstream dependency in handle_result), the queue pool grows without bound and the consumer OOMs; the documented guarantee the mode was accepted under does not exist in the implementation.

[ADVISORY] get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash(), which is salt-randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the docstring's 'consistent hashing' only holds within a single process lifetime. The group→queue mapping differs between replicas and between restarts; per-group ordering survives only because mapping stability is never needed across process boundaries, but anyone extending this to multi-process consumption or relying on mapping stability (e.g., for cache affinity) gets silently inconsistent assignment; a stable hash (e.g., md5/mod) is the standard fix.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool (and its N daemon worker threads) is constructed eagerly in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ rather than in create_with_partitions, so threads spin up before any consumer strategy exists. Every factory instantiated in thread-queue-parallel mode pays 20 (or max_workers) live threads even if create_with_partitions is never called or the process exits before consuming; this also silently reorders initialization by moving result_processor_cls() instantiation to the top of __init__, changing construction order for every existing mode in the same diff.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is dead code — no call site exists anywhere in the diff. Unused polling helper invites drift with get_stats; deleting it removes a maintenance surface, per the deletion test.

[ADVISORY] The --max-workers help text was broadened to 'the maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode', but in thread-queue-parallel mode it actually means the number of independent queues (and silently falls back to 20 when unset), a third distinct semantic for the same flag. Operators tuning max_workers based on the flag's original thread-pool meaning get a different resource profile (queue count vs thread count) with no way to see the effective value; the mode list plus this fallback hardcodes 20 as an unconfigurable, undocumented default.

[ADVISORY] All new thread-queue-parallel tests patch out type(factory.result_processor).__call__, so the real result-processing logic (the behavior this mode exists to run) is never exercised; the tests only assert that a mock was invoked with certain arguments. The new mode's tests verify queue plumbing/routing but the actual handler is a mock; any real bug in how results flow through the worker (e.g. wrong argument passed as `result`, swallowed exceptions being counted as success) passes the suite. Regression in the real processor under this mode would not be caught by these tests, and the 'assert mock was called N times' pattern also can't distinguish successful processing from the worker's broad `except Exception` path that logs and continues.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown asserts only `factory.queue_pool is None` and never verifies that workers stopped, pending items were drained or dropped, or that the strategy was closed. The test passes as long as shutdown() nulls the attribute — a shutdown that leaks running worker threads, deadlocks on join, or drops in-flight messages would still pass. Additionally, the ProcessingStrategy returned by create_with_partitions is never closed, so SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit thread (only stopped in close()) is leaked as a daemon thread in every test in this file that never calls consumer.close().

[ADVISORY] The exception branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (decoder/grouping raising, caught by the bare `except Exception` that marks the offset complete) has no test — test_handles_invalid_messages only exercises the FilteredPayload→None path, not a raising decoder. A decoder bug that raises causes the message's offset to be silently marked complete and committed with no processing and no test coverage; a regression in this error path (e.g. failing to complete the offset, which would stall commits forever, or the assert on BrokerValue firing before the isinstance guard) would ship unnoticed. Related untested lifecycle paths: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate(), join(), and FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty have zero test references.

[ADVISORY] test_stats_reporting asserts stats["total_items"] > 0 immediately after submitting, racing the worker threads that may have already drained the queues. Flaky test: if workers drain the 10 items before the main thread calls get_stats(), the first assertion fails intermittently in CI; the assertion checks a transient state rather than a guaranteed one.

[ADVISORY] test_different_groups_distributed asserts exactly 3 distinct queue indices from 20 hash assignments, a probabilistic claim (P(all 3 buckets hit) ≈ 0.9995 with randomized string hashing) rather than a property of the code. Occasional flaky failure under PYTHONHASHSEED variation; the test should assert distribution is bounded (e.g. >= 2 buckets) since even distribution is not a guarantee of `hash() % n`.

[ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset even when result_processor raises, so failed messages are committed to Kafka and permanently lost (the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts no commit occurs, contradicting the code path). Any transient error processing an uptime result marks the offset complete; the commit loop then advances past it, so the result is never retried and check-status/incident data for that check is silently dropped.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run marks an offset as complete in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so the commit loop advances past the failed message. A result whose processing throws (DB error, bug in handle_result) is logged and then permanently dropped: complete_offset runs in finally, get_committable_offsets treats the offset as processed, and the offset is committed to Kafka, so the message is never redelivered. This directly contradicts the class contract 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and makes the failure invisible — the consumer reports progress while losing work. Note the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite behavior (no commit after failure), which this implementation violates, so either the test or the code is wrong.

[BUG] The except path in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit silently marks a failed decode/submit as fully processed, committing its offset. Any exception in self.decoder (malformed payload, schema mismatch) or the assert on message.value is swallowed: the offset is added and immediately completed, the commit loop commits it, and the message is dropped with only a log line — an API-contract-shaped silent partial success where malformed data is reported as consumed.

[BUG] queue.ShutDown and queue.Queue.shutdown() only exist in Python 3.13+; on older runtimes the worker loop and shutdown path raise AttributeError. On Python < 3.13, the first loop iteration's `except queue.ShutDown` clause evaluation raises AttributeError inside run(), and FixedQueuePool.shutdown()'s `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raises AttributeError on every queue (caught and logged, but workers are then never woken and join(timeout=5.0) stalls the full 5s per shutdown while worker threads spin forever on a closed-by-other-means... or hang on get()). The new 'thread-queue-parallel' mode would fail every graceful shutdown on any supported interpreter older than 3.13.

[ADVISORY] The strategy advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but work_queue is an unbounded queue.Queue, so there is no backpressure. If workers are slower than the consumer (slow downstream writes in result_processor), queues grow without bound while arroyo keeps fetching; memory exhaustion on the consumer process during lag spikes. The docstring is an unexamined assumption a future operator will trust.

[ADVISORY] ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() shuts down the queue_pool but never stops the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit thread, which holds the only handle to shutdown_event. When the factory is torn down directly (as all the new tests do via factory.shutdown()), the strategy's _commit_loop thread keeps running every second and invokes the arroyo commit callback against a consumer that is being closed, and the daemon thread leaks until process exit — the same shutdown path behaves differently depending on whether strategy.close() or factory.shutdown() is the caller.

[ADVISORY] A single result_processor instance is now created in __init__ and shared across all worker threads in thread-queue-parallel mode with no thread-safety requirement stated or enforced. ResultProcessor implementations written for serial/parallel modes (where each strategy instance processed via one thread or via multiprocessing pickling) may carry instance state; with N workers concurrently calling __call__ on the same object, shared-state corruption (e.g., cached subscription lookups, counters) occurs silently. The next author adding a cached field to a ResultProcessor gets bitten.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash() on strings, which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so group-to-queue assignment is not stable across processes or restarts. Each consumer process maps the same group_key to a different queue index; correctness holds within a process, but any future reasoning, debugging, or per-queue routing assumption keyed to 'group X lives on queue Y' breaks nondeterministically between restarts, and hash-based skew can pile hot groups onto one queue since hash distribution across % num_queues is unmonitored.

[ADVISORY] Each worker emits a queue_depth gauge metric on every single processed item in its finally block. On a high-throughput uptime-results topic this multiplies metrics ingest by message volume (one gauge submission per message per worker), adding hot-path overhead and metric cardinality that the once-per-second poll() gauge already covers; a saturation event amplifies telemetry exactly when the system is most loaded.

[ADVISORY] The submit() except handler checks isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue) but the earlier assert at line 285 already guarantees it on the success path; on the failure path for a non-BrokerValue the offset is neither tracked nor completed, leaving the strategy's tracking inconsistent with what arroyo will do with the message. For a message whose value is not a BrokerValue (e.g., certain FilteredPayload shapes), a decode-side exception leaves the offset permanently outstanding in the tracker: the partition's commit frontier stalls behind it forever (get_committable_offsets breaks at the gap), silently freezing offset commits for that partition until restart.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `OffsetTracker`, offsets are accumulated in `all_offsets[partition]` and only pruned in `mark_committed` (which requires commit progress). If any offset remains permanently outstanding (e.g., a work item never completes), `get_committable_offsets` will never advance `last_committed`, so `all_offsets` will retain every subsequent offset added via `add_offset`, causing unbounded memory growth for that partition. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The --max-workers help text was broadened to 'the maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode', but in thread-queue-parallel mode it actually means the number of independent queues (and silently falls back to 20 when unset), a third distinct semantic for the same flag. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] All new thread-queue-parallel tests patch out type(factory.result_processor).__call__, so the real result-processing logic (the behavior this mode exists to run) is never exercised; the tests only assert that a mock was invoked with certain arguments. The new mode's tests verify queue plumbing/routing but the actual handler is a mock; any real bug in how results flow through the worker (e.g. wrong argument passed as `result`, swallowed exceptions being counted as success) passes the suite. Regression in the real processor under this mode would not be caught by these tests, and the 'assert mock was called N times' pattern also can't distinguish successful processing from the worker's broad `except Exception` path that logs and continues.

adjudication.rationale: In the new uptime consumer tests for the added mode (e.g. `test_thread_queue_parallel`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order`, `..._offset_commit`, `..._error_handling`, etc.), the PR consistently does `with mock.patch.object(type(factory.result_processor), "__call__") ...` and then asserts call counts/arguments. That means the real `ResultProcessor` behavior under `thread-queue-parallel` (beyond “__call__ got invoked”) is not exercised by those mode-specific tests, and the assertions can’t distinguish a successful run from the worker’s broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` path in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` (which still completes the offset in `finally`). However, it is not literally true that *all* new thread-queue-parallel tests do this, since `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py` uses a real `result_processor` function for the queue/strategy unit tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown asserts only `factory.queue_pool is None` and never verifies that workers stopped, pending items were drained or dropped, or that the strategy was closed. The test passes as long as shutdown() nulls the attribute — a shutdown that leaks running worker threads, deadlocks on join, or drops in-flight messages would still pass. Additionally, the ProcessingStrategy returned by create_with_partitions is never closed, so SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit thread (only stopped in close()) is leaked as a daemon thread in every test in this file that never calls consumer.close().

adjudication.rationale: The new `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py` only calls `factory.shutdown()` and asserts `factory.queue_pool is None`, without checking worker termination, queue drain/drop behavior, or that the returned `ProcessingStrategy` was closed. In the implementation, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__` starts a daemon `commit_thread`, and it is only stopped/joined in `close()` (or partially in `terminate()` which does not join). Multiple tests assign the strategy to `consumer = factory.create_with_partitions(...)` and never call `consumer.close()`/`terminate()`, so the commit thread can be left running. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test/resource-cleanup gap rather than a proven production correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The exception branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (decoder/grouping raising, caught by the bare `except Exception` that marks the offset complete) has no test — test_handles_invalid_messages only exercises the FilteredPayload→None path, not a raising decoder. A decoder bug that raises causes the message's offset to be silently marked complete and committed with no processing and no test coverage; a regression in this error path (e.g. failing to complete the offset, which would stall commits forever, or the assert on BrokerValue firing before the isinstance guard) would ship unnoticed. Related untested lifecycle paths: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate(), join(), and FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty have zero test references.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new error-handling path in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`: a broad `except Exception` logs and then (if `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`) calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, meaning a decoder/grouping failure will still advance offset tracking and can lead to committing without processing. The new tests cover the `FilteredPayload -> None` path (`test_handles_invalid_messages`) but do not cover a decoder that raises (or grouping_fn raising), so regressions in this branch (e.g., not completing offsets and stalling commits, or behavior around `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` vs the guard in the exception block) would not be caught. The mentioned lifecycle methods (`terminate`, `join`) and `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` also appear unreferenced by the added tests. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test-coverage gap rather than a directly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_stats_reporting asserts stats["total_items"] > 0 immediately after submitting, racing the worker threads that may have already drained the queues. Flaky test: if workers drain the 10 items before the main thread calls get_stats(), the first assertion fails intermittently in CI; the assertion checks a transient state rather than a guaranteed one.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting`, the test submits 10 items and then immediately calls `stats = self.pool.get_stats()` and asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. Because `FixedQueuePool` starts worker threads immediately in `__init__` and workers can drain the underlying `queue.Queue` quickly, `get_stats()` (which reads `q.qsize()`) may legitimately return `0` by the time it is called, making the assertion racey/flaky as described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_different_groups_distributed asserts exactly 3 distinct queue indices from 20 hash assignments, a probabilistic claim (P(all 3 buckets hit) ≈ 0.9995 with randomized string hashing) rather than a property of the code. Occasional flaky failure under PYTHONHASHSEED variation; the test should assert distribution is bounded (e.g. >= 2 buckets) since even distribution is not a guarantee of `hash() % n`.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::test_different_groups_distributed`, the test computes `hash(group_key) % self.pool.num_queues` for 20 different strings and then asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` when `num_queues=3`. Because Python’s `hash()` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) and the mapping is not guaranteed to hit all buckets for any finite sample, this assertion is probabilistic and can be flaky even though the production code behaves as intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset even when result_processor raises, so failed messages are committed to Kafka and permanently lost (the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts no commit occurs, contradicting the code path). Any transient error processing an uptime result marks the offset complete; the commit loop then advances past it, so the result is never retried and check-status/incident data for that check is silently dropped.

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` even when `result_processor(...)` raises (the exception is caught and only logged). Since `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` considers an offset committable once it is no longer outstanding, the commit thread in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop()` can advance commits past failed messages, causing them to be permanently skipped (data loss). This also conflicts with the intent of `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts no commit occurs on processing failure, but the code path does not prevent completion/commit on error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run marks an offset as complete in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so the commit loop advances past the failed message. A result whose processing throws (DB error, bug in handle_result) is logged and then permanently dropped: complete_offset runs in finally, get_committable_offsets treats the offset as processed, and the offset is committed to Kafka, so the message is never redelivered. This directly contradicts the class contract 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and makes the failure invisible — the consumer reports progress while losing work. Note the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite behavior (no commit after failure), which this implementation violates, so either the test or the code is wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` is executed in the `finally` block unconditionally, even when `result_processor(...)` raises and is caught by `except Exception` (it only logs). Because offsets are added on submit (`FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `add_offset`) and the commit loop (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`) commits any offsets no longer in `outstanding`, a failed work item will still be treated as processed and can become committable and be committed to Kafka. This contradicts the stated guarantee in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring (“Only commits offsets after successful processing”) and would also conflict with the added test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` which expects no commit after a processing exception.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The except path in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit silently marks a failed decode/submit as fully processed, committing its offset. Any exception in self.decoder (malformed payload, schema mismatch) or the assert on message.value is swallowed: the offset is added and immediately completed, the commit loop commits it, and the message is dropped with only a log line — an API-contract-shaped silent partial success where malformed data is reported as consumed.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the broad `except Exception` logs and then (when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`) calls `add_offset(...)` followed immediately by `complete_offset(...)`. This makes the offset immediately committable by `_commit_loop`, so any decode/assert/submit exception will result in the message being dropped while its offset can still be committed. Additionally, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block even if `result_processor(...)` raises, so processing failures inside the worker are also treated as completed for commit purposes. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and can cause data loss (failed messages marked consumed).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] queue.ShutDown and queue.Queue.shutdown() only exist in Python 3.13+; on older runtimes the worker loop and shutdown path raise AttributeError. On Python < 3.13, the first loop iteration's `except queue.ShutDown` clause evaluation raises AttributeError inside run(), and FixedQueuePool.shutdown()'s `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raises AttributeError on every queue (caught and logged, but workers are then never woken and join(timeout=5.0) stalls the full 5s per shutdown while worker threads spin forever on a closed-by-other-means... or hang on get()). The new 'thread-queue-parallel' mode would fail every graceful shutdown on any supported interpreter older than 3.13.

adjudication.rationale: The new implementation in `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py` explicitly uses `except queue.ShutDown:` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` and calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. Those APIs are not part of `queue.Queue`/`queue` in older Python versions, so on runtimes without them the shutdown path will raise `AttributeError` (the `q.shutdown` call is caught and logged, but then nothing wakes threads blocked on `work_queue.get()`), and the worker loop’s `except queue.ShutDown` is also invalid. This makes the added `thread-queue-parallel` mode’s graceful shutdown broken on such interpreters.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The strategy advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but work_queue is an unbounded queue.Queue, so there is no backpressure. If workers are slower than the consumer (slow downstream writes in result_processor), queues grow without bound while arroyo keeps fetching; memory exhaustion on the consumer process during lag spikes. The docstring is an unexamined assumption a future operator will trust.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each `work_queue` is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, making it unbounded. `FixedQueuePool.submit` then does `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will not block for an unbounded queue, so the `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` will continue accepting submissions while workers lag. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and can lead to unbounded memory growth under slow `result_processor` / lag spikes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() shuts down the queue_pool but never stops the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit thread, which holds the only handle to shutdown_event. When the factory is torn down directly (as all the new tests do via factory.shutdown()), the strategy's _commit_loop thread keeps running every second and invokes the arroyo commit callback against a consumer that is being closed, and the daemon thread leaks until process exit — the same shutdown path behaves differently depending on whether strategy.close() or factory.shutdown() is the caller.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__`, a daemon `commit_thread` is started and runs `_commit_loop` until `self.shutdown_event` is set (only done in `close()`/`terminate()`). `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` (in `result_consumer.py`) only calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and sets `self.queue_pool = None`, but it does not (and cannot, per the diff) signal/stop any `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` instance’s `shutdown_event` or join its `commit_thread`. Many new tests construct a strategy via `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` and then call `factory.shutdown()` without calling `strategy.close()`, so the strategy’s commit loop thread will keep waking every second and may continue calling the provided commit callback after teardown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A single result_processor instance is now created in __init__ and shared across all worker threads in thread-queue-parallel mode with no thread-safety requirement stated or enforced. ResultProcessor implementations written for serial/parallel modes (where each strategy instance processed via one thread or via multiprocessing pickling) may carry instance state; with N workers concurrently calling __call__ on the same object, shared-state corruption (e.g., cached subscription lookups, counters) occurs silently. The next author adding a cached field to a ResultProcessor gets bitten.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that a single `ResultProcessor` instance is constructed once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (`self.result_processor = self.result_processor_cls()`) and, in `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"`, is passed into `FixedQueuePool(result_processor=self.result_processor, ...)`. `FixedQueuePool` starts multiple `OrderedQueueWorker` threads, each calling `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` concurrently. The diff does not state/enforce any thread-safety requirement or create per-thread/per-queue processor instances. Whether this is an actual correctness bug depends on `ResultProcessor` implementations (not shown), but the shared mutable-state risk is a concrete, diff-grounded design concern introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash() on strings, which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so group-to-queue assignment is not stable across processes or restarts. Each consumer process maps the same group_key to a different queue index; correctness holds within a process, but any future reasoning, debugging, or per-queue routing assumption keyed to 'group X lives on queue Y' breaks nondeterministically between restarts, and hash-based skew can pile hot groups onto one queue since hash distribution across % num_queues is unmonitored.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` implemented as `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` (in `queue_consumer.py`). Python’s built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized per process (affected by `PYTHONHASHSEED`), so the queue index for a given `group_key` is not stable across restarts/processes. This doesn’t break correctness within a single running consumer (ordering per group is still preserved because the mapping is consistent within the process), but it is a real operational/design concern for reproducibility/debugging and any assumption that “group X always maps to queue Y” across restarts, and makes distribution harder to reason about/monitor.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Each worker emits a queue_depth gauge metric on every single processed item in its finally block. On a high-throughput uptime-results topic this multiplies metrics ingest by message volume (one gauge submission per message per worker), adding hot-path overhead and metric cardinality that the once-per-second poll() gauge already covers; a saturation event amplifies telemetry exactly when the system is most loaded.

adjudication.rationale: Verified in diff: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` emits `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", self.work_queue.qsize(), ...)` in the `finally` block for every processed item (new file `queue_consumer.py`). Separately, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` emits a once-per-poll gauge `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.total_queued`. The finding’s concern about per-message metric emission overhead/telemetry amplification is grounded in this code path; it’s not a correctness defect but a performance/observability design issue introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The submit() except handler checks isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue) but the earlier assert at line 285 already guarantees it on the success path; on the failure path for a non-BrokerValue the offset is neither tracked nor completed, leaving the strategy's tracking inconsistent with what arroyo will do with the message. For a message whose value is not a BrokerValue (e.g., certain FilteredPayload shapes), a decode-side exception leaves the offset permanently outstanding in the tracker: the partition's commit frontier stalls behind it forever (get_committable_offsets breaks at the gap), silently freezing offset commits for that partition until restart.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, offsets are only ever added to `OffsetTracker` via `add_offset` when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue` (either on the normal path after the `assert`, in the `result is None` path, or in the `except` handler guarded by `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`). If `message.value` is not a `BrokerValue` and an exception occurs before any `add_offset` call (notably `decoder(message.payload)` is executed before the `assert`), then the offset is never tracked at all—so it cannot become “permanently outstanding” and cannot create a tracked “gap” that stalls `get_committable_offsets()` as claimed. The finding’s core claim about an offset being left outstanding in the tracker for a non-`BrokerValue` message is not supported by the diff.
